lead: A square-wave inverter has a fixed output: the full-bridge fundamental is always 4V<sub>dc</sub>/π peak. To vary it without changing the bus, the bridge leaves the load at zero volts for part of each half cycle. In single-pulse modulation each half cycle holds one pulse of adjustable width; in multiple-pulse modulation it holds p equal, equally spaced pulses. Both control the voltage with switches that are fully on or fully off, so the efficiency stays high. They are the first step from square-wave inverters to PWM.
prereq: You need: the full-bridge square wave and its Fourier series from single-phase bridges.

sections.h3: Why the square wave needs control

blocks.text: An AC motor needs its voltage to rise with frequency, a UPS must hold its output while the battery runs down, and a heater needs adjustable power. All three need a variable fundamental from a fixed V<sub>dc</sub>. The full bridge can apply +V<sub>dc</sub>, −V<sub>dc</sub> or zero (S1 and S3 on, or S2 and S4 on), so the trick is to insert zero intervals. This is called pulse-width modulation (PWM) in general; with one or a few pulses per half cycle the frequency of switching stays low.

Let the positive half cycle be +V<sub>dc</sub> for a pulse of width 2d centred on 90°, and zero for the rest; the negative half cycle mirrors it. The zero interval of width π − 2d therefore straddles each zero crossing of the output. The gate pulses come from comparing a rectangular reference of amplitude A<sub>r</sub> with a triangular carrier of amplitude A<sub>c</sub> at twice the output frequency; the modulation index M = A<sub>r</sub>/A<sub>c</sub> sets 2d = M × 180°.

blocks.where: V<sub>rms</sub> is the rms output in volts and d is half the pulse width in radians (2d/π = 2d°/180°).

blocks.text: bn = (4Vdc/nπ) sin(nd), n = 1, 3, 5, … bn is the peak of the nth harmonic in volts. At 2d = 180° this is the square wave; at 2d = 0 the output is zero.

The fundamental follows sin d, not d: near full width a large change of width changes the fundamental very little. A harmonic vanishes when nd = π, so a pulse 120° wide (d = 60°) removes the 3rd harmonic. At low outputs, though, the 3rd, 5th and 7th are large compared with the fundamental, so single-pulse control gives a poor waveform at low voltage.

Raise the carrier frequency so that it gives p equal pulses per half cycle, each 2d wide and centred at γ<sub>k</sub> = (k − ½)180°/p. The carrier runs at f<sub>c</sub> = 2pf, and each pulse width is 2d = M × 180°/p. Some syllabi call this symmetric or uniform PWM.

blocks.where: With d in degrees the on fraction is 2pd/180.

blocks.text: bn = (4Vdc/nπ) sin(nd) Σ sin(nγk) The sum runs over the p pulse centres γk of one half cycle.

For the same total on-time the rms is the same as with one pulse, but the spectrum changes: the strongest harmonics move to orders 2p − 1 and 2p + 1, near the carrier, where a smaller filter removes them. The lower harmonics are smaller than in single-pulse control but do not vanish. The price is switching loss: p pulses per half cycle mean 2p pulses and 4p switching edges per cycle.

figure.caption: The first worked example on a 200 V bus. Top: one 60° pulse per half cycle gives 115.5 V rms and a 127.3 V peak fundamental. Bottom: four 10° pulses per half cycle give 94.3 V rms and a 58.0 V fundamental; the pulses are spread over the half cycle, so their strongest harmonics are the 7th and 9th.

spec.aria: Two waveforms over one cycle. In the top one each half cycle has a single 200 volt pulse 60 degrees wide centred on the peak, with a fundamental sine of 127.3 volts drawn over it. In the bottom one each half cycle has four 10 degree pulses, with a 58 volt fundamental.

examples.question: A full bridge has V<sub>dc</sub> = 200 V and a 50 Hz output. (a) With single-pulse modulation and d = 30° (a 60° pulse), find the fundamental peak, the rms output and the 3rd harmonic. (b) It is changed to 4 equal pulses per half cycle, each 10° wide. Find the modulation index, the carrier frequency, the rms output, the fundamental and the strongest harmonics.
steps: b<sub>3</sub> = (254.65/3) × sin 90° = 84.9 V peak, which is 67 % of the fundamental.
(b) Each pulse can be at most 180°/4 = 45° wide, so M = 10/45 = 0.222; the carrier runs at 2pf = 2 × 4 × 50 = 400 Hz.
Total on-time per half cycle = 4 × 10° = 40°, so V<sub>rms</sub> = 200√(40/180) = 94.3 V.

The same formula gives b<sub>3</sub> = 23.8 V, b<sub>5</sub> = 23.3 V, b<sub>7</sub> = 54.5 V and b<sub>9</sub> = 52.3 V: the strongest harmonics are the 7th and 9th (2p ∓ 1), at 94 % and 90 % of the fundamental.
examples.answer: (a) 127.3 V fundamental peak, 115.5 V rms, 3rd harmonic 84.9 V. (b) M = 0.222, f<sub>c</sub> = 400 Hz, V<sub>rms</sub> = 94.3 V, fundamental 58.0 V peak, strongest harmonics the 7th and 9th.

examples.question: A single-pulse full bridge with V<sub>dc</sub> = 220 V must give a fundamental of 150 V rms. Find the pulse width, the rms output and the THD.
steps: d = sin⁻¹ 0.7573 = 49.23°, so the pulse is 2d = 98.5° wide.
Check one harmonic: b<sub>3</sub> = (4 × 220/3π) sin(3 × 49.23°), which is 35.3 V rms, 23.5 % of the fundamental.

traps: Set the calculator to degrees for sin 30°, or convert d to radians first; in V<sub>rms</sub> = V<sub>dc</sub>√(2d/π) d must be in radians.
d is half the pulse width. A "60° pulse" means d = 30°, so the fundamental is (4V<sub>dc</sub>/π) sin 30°, not sin 60°.
The fundamental falls as sin d, not in proportion to the width; near full width it hardly changes.
p counts pulses per half cycle. A full cycle has 2p pulses and 4p switching edges.
Multiple pulses do not change the rms for the same total on-time; they move the strongest harmonics to 2p ± 1.

quiz.q: What is single-pulse modulation of an inverter?
quiz.a: Each half cycle of the output holds one pulse of width 2d centred on the peak, with zero voltage on either side of each zero crossing; changing 2d changes the fundamental with V<sub>dc</sub> fixed.

quiz.q: Why does a 120° wide single pulse contain no 3rd harmonic?
quiz.a: b<sub>3</sub> ∝ sin 3d. With 2d = 120°, d = 60° and sin 180° = 0, so the 3rd harmonic is zero.

quiz.q: A full bridge has V<sub>dc</sub> = 300 V and a single pulse 90° wide. Find the fundamental peak and the rms output.
A full bridge has V<sub>dc</sub> = 250 V and 3 equal pulses per half cycle, each 15° wide, at 50 Hz output. Find the rms output and the carrier frequency.
quiz.a: On-time 45° per half cycle: V<sub>rms</sub> = 250√(45/180) = 125 V. f<sub>c</sub> = 2pf = 2 × 3 × 50 = 300 Hz.

quiz.q: Going from 2 to 6 pulses per half cycle at the same total on-time, what happens to the rms, the strongest harmonics and the switching loss?
quiz.a: The rms is unchanged. The strongest harmonics move from the 3rd and 5th to the 11th and 13th. The switching edges per cycle rise from 8 to 24, so switching loss rises about three times.

quiz.q: Why is single-pulse control poor at low output voltage?
quiz.a: For small d the fundamental is about (4V<sub>dc</sub>/π)d, but the 3rd, 5th and 7th are each about the same size, (4V<sub>dc</sub>/nπ)·nd; so the harmonics become as large as the fundamental and the THD rises sharply.

quiz.q: Give another name used for multiple-pulse modulation.

beyond: Not for the exam. Few-pulse patterns are still used where the switching frequency must stay low, as in megawatt drives and traction, where the pulse positions are optimised instead of evenly spaced. Search for synchronous optimal PWM and quasi-square-wave inverters.
